analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 猴痘病毒(MPXV)的再次流行凸显了开发可扩展且对突变具有抗性的对策的迫切需求。传统经验性疫苗的缓慢开发周期阻碍了其发现,而常规疫苗学往往产生高假阳性率,因为其依赖静态、线性序列筛选。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究设计了一个先进的、AI增强的疫苗发现流程,针对MPXV蛋白组中最致命的组分。
analysis_zh.methods: 该流程系统筛选了八个关键的病毒靶标,这些靶标对于病毒复制、膜形态发生和宿主细胞进入至关重要,以绘制高度保守的T细胞和B细胞表位。部署了ESM-2蛋白质语言模型、MHCflurry集成模型和基于结构的图神经网络,以验证结构自然性、现实免疫原性和制造动力学。
analysis_zh.main_results: 多层管道成功生成了三个结构优化的、多表位疫苗构建体,这些构建体针对全球人口的最大覆盖进行了优化。ESM-2结构验证确认了异常低的困惑度分数,表明类似天然的稳定性。基于GNN的免疫突触建模显示了高度稳定的结合动力学和强大的结合自由能。基于RNN的动力学优化表明,cDNA序列在高产表达方面进行了优化,而不会导致核糖体停滞的风险。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究建立了一个深度学习增强的框架,弥合了理论序列优化与生物制药可扩展性之间的差距。通过验证疫苗嵌合体的结构自然性、现实免疫原性和制造动力学,该框架提供了一种稳健且主动的范式,用于快速构建针对新兴正痘病毒威胁的疫苗架构。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该框架可用于快速开发针对新兴正痘病毒威胁的疫苗,增强全球应对和响应能力。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究未报告局限性或证据强度评估。

papers.title: HECA-YOLOv11: A High-Accuracy Hybrid Attention Network for Real-Time Monkeypox Skin Lesion Detection with Interpretability
papers.abstract: Introduction: The global outbreak risk of monkeypox necessitates efficient diagnostic tools. Current methods are slow and struggle to differentiate similar skin lesions, while deep learning models lack both accuracy and interpretability for multi-class classification. This study aims to develop a high-performance, real-time screening tool for early detection of monkeypox and similar conditions. Methods: This study proposes an enhanced architecture that incorporates the Highly Efficient Channel Attention (HECA) mechanism into YOLOv11 to improve feature selection. HECA performs Global Average Pooling (GAP) and Max Average Pooling (MAP) on input feature maps. Using spatial transformations and pixel-domain enhancements, the research establishes and augments a four-class dataset containing monkeypox, measles, chickenpox, and normal skin images. Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) generates heatmaps for lesion localization visualization, while a PyQt5-based interactive diagnostic interface streamlines clinical workflows. Results: Experimental results demonstrate the proposed model’s superior performance compared to existing approaches (EfficientNet-v2-l, GoogLeNet, ResNet50, VGG19, MobileNetv2, DenseNet201, and YOLOv11s) on the test set, with enhanced detection speed, accuracy (98.9%), precision (99%), recall (99.3%), and F1-score (99.1%). HECA-YOLOv11 outperforms SE-YOLOv11 and ECA-YOLOv11 by over 5.1% across all evaluation metrics. Heatmap analysis confirms the model’s focus on lesion regions, aligning with medical reasoning. Discussion: The integrated attention mechanism and interpretability techniques effectively address key limitations in automated skin lesion detection. The high performance and low latency signify a major advancement towards reliable clinical decision support, with important implications for early outbreak containment. Conclusion: The HECA-YOLOv11 framework provides a highly accurate and efficient tool for early monkeypox screening. Its standardized interface holds significant potential to accelerate public health responses and improve global control of emerging infectious diseases.
papers.journal: Recent Advances in Computer Science and Communications

analysis.study_design_and_population: The authors developed and evaluated a deep learning framework (HECA-YOLOv11) designed for real-time screening of mpox and similar skin lesions using a four-class image dataset.
analysis.methods: The proposed architecture integrates a Highly Efficient Channel Attention (HECA) mechanism into YOLOv11, applying Global Average Pooling and Max Average Pooling to input feature maps, and augments a dataset containing monkeypox, measles, chickenpox, and normal skin images using spatial transformations and pixel-domain enhancements.
analysis.main_results: On the test set, HECA-YOLOv11 achieved 98.9% accuracy, 99% precision, 99.3% recall, and 99.1% F1-score, outperforming EfficientNet-v2-l, GoogLeNet, ResNet50, VGG19, MobileNetv2, DenseNet201, YOLOv11s, SE-YOLOv11, and ECA-YOLOv11 by over 5.1% across all metrics.

Heatmap analysis via Grad-CAM confirmed lesion-focused attention, and a PyQt5 interface was developed to streamline clinical workflows. The authors argue this represents a major advancement toward reliable clinical decision support for early mpox screening and could accelerate public health responses. However, the abstract-only evidence lacks dataset size, external validation, and prospective clinical evaluation, constraining generalisability and evidence strength.

papers.abstract_zh: 简介:全球 暴发 猴痘风险需要高效的诊断工具。目前的方法速度缓慢,并且难以区分相似的皮肤病变,而深度学习模型缺乏多类分类的准确性和可解释性。本研究旨在开发一种高性能、实时筛查工具,用于早期检测猴痘和类似病症。方法:本研究提出了一种增强的架构,将高效通道注意力(HECA)机制纳入 YOLOv11 中,以改进特征选择。HECA 对输入特征图执行全局平均池化 (GAP) 和最大平均池化 (MAP)。该研究利用空间变换和像素域增强,建立并增强了包含猴痘、麻疹、水痘和正常皮肤图像的四类数据集。梯度加权类激活映射 (Grad-CAM) 生成用于病变定位可视化的热图,而基于 PyQt5 的交互式诊断界面则简化了临床工作流程。结果:实验结果表明,与测试集上的现有方法(EfficientNet-v2-l、GoogLeNet、ResNet50、VGG19、MobileNetv2、DenseNet201 和 YOLOv11s)相比,所提出的模型具有优越的性能,具有增强的检测速度、准确度(98.9%)、精确度(99%)、召回率(99.3%)和 F1 分数(99.1%)。在所有评估指标中,HECA-YOLOv11 的性能均优于 SE-YOLOv11 和 ECA-YOLOv11 超过 5.1%。热图分析证实了该模型对病变区域的关注,与医学推理相一致。讨论:集成的注意力机制和可解释性技术有效地解决了自动皮肤病变检测的关键限制。高性能和低延迟标志着可靠临床决策支持的重大进步,对早期 暴发 遏制具有重要意义。结论:HECA-YOLOv11框架为早期猴痘筛查提供了高度准确和高效的工具。其标准化界面在加速公共卫生应对和改善新发传染病的全球控制方面具有巨大潜力。

papers.title: Healthcare Workers’ Preparedness for Monkeypox Pandemic Response in SubSaharan Africa: A Rapid Review Investigating the Knowledge Gap
papers.abstract: Background: Mpox is a zoonotic viral disease caused by an Orthopoxvirus endemic to sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where its resurgence underscores the urgent need for improved preparedness among health care workers (HCWs). Despite the potential of a One Health approach, current implementations remain fragmented. This rapid review synthesises evidence on HCWs' knowledge, attitudes, information sources, and barriers to preparedness regarding Mpox in SSA to identify training needs and policy implications. Methods: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, PubMed and ScienceDirect were searched using MeSH terms and Boolean operators for studies published between 2000 and 2024. Studies assessing HCW knowledge, attitudes, or preparedness for Mpox in SSA with full-text availability in English or French were included; those involving non-HCW populations, conducted outside SSA, or lacking primary data were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data using a standardised template; quality was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical CrossSectional Studies. Results: Five studies from 388 records were included (Cameroon, Ethiopia, Nigeria, DRC; n = 1,672 HCWs). Only 46.8% of HCWs demonstrated adequate Mpox knowledge. Barriers included reliance on social media and limited access to formal training. Positive attitudes towards prevention correlated with higher knowledge levels. Conclusion: Fewer than half of SSA HCWs demonstrate adequate Mpox knowledge despite a regional case fatality rate nearly ten times the global average; positive attitudes are not translating into clinical preparedness, reflecting a critical intention-action gap; and social media dominates as an information source, underscoring the need for peer-reviewed alternatives within a One Health training framework.
papers.journal: Journal of Clinical Virology and Translational Research

analysis.summary_en: This rapid review examines healthcare workers' (HCWs) preparedness for monkeypox (Mpox) pandemic response in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The review highlights that only 46.8% of HCWs have adequate knowledge about Mpox, despite its high case fatality rate in the region. Barriers to preparedness include reliance on social media for information and limited access to formal training. Positive attitudes towards prevention are associated with higher knowledge levels, but these attitudes do not translate into clinical preparedness, indicating an intention-action gap. The review underscores the need for peer-reviewed information sources and a structured One Health training framework to address these gaps. The findings suggest that targeted training and policy interventions are essential to improve HCW readiness for Mpox outbreaks in SSA.

papers.full_text: Monkeypox Related Keratouveitis: A Case Report Published 2026 - 44th Congress of the ESCRS Reference: POCOR019 | Type: Case Report | DOI: 10.82333/dcn1-x864 Authors: Dr Assaf Almalki* 1 , Dr Majed Alsubaie 1 , Dr Talal Aljudi 1 1Ophthalmology,Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital,Dhahran,Saudi Arabia Purpose The purpose of this case report is to present the clinical course and management of a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratitis in the right eye. Aiming to highlight therapeutic interventions and initial outcomes of a patient with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis. Setting This case was presented and managed at Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital (DESH). The patient presented to the emergency room (ER) with severe sub-acute ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. Prior to his presentation, the patient was diagnosed with Monkeypox with skin manifestations in another hospital. Report of case A 34-year-old male with a history of Monkeypox 2 months prior to presenting to the ER with a complaint of right eye swelling, pain, redness, tearing, photophobia, and decrease of VA. The patient had visited other centers with limited improvement. His VA was CF2ft, and IOP of 28, the SLE showed moderate conjunctival injection, corneal haze, inferior crescent shaped stromal infiltrate with CED of 2* 4 mm, the anterior chamber had +2 mixed cells with flare, no clear view to the iris or fundus. B-scan revealed a flat retina, no choroidal thickening, and quiet posterior segment. Our impression was Herpetic versus Monkeypox-related Keratouveitis. Oral Valacyclovir, Topical Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol were started, with close F/U. During subsequent visits, the patient had reported improvement, however, the clinical picture remained the same initially. 1 month later, CED was healed and the vision improved to 20\400 and 20\200. Cyclopentolate was switched to Cyclosporine at one point, and the patient was stabilized by the 3-month mark. Awaiting full stabilization to consider PKP. Conclusion/Take home message This case emphasises the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings, leading to early recognition and management. It also highlights the multimodal treatment methods of combining systemic and topical medications. Close follow-up role is demonstrated in this case, as it allowed adaptive therapy and management of complications. Consideration of surgical intervention for better visual potential.

papers.title_original: Monkeypox Related Keratouveitis: A Case Report

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to highlight therapeutic interventions and initial outcomes of a patient with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a case report of a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratitis in the right eye, presented and managed at Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital. The patient had a history of Monkeypox with skin manifestations 2 months prior to presenting with ocular symptoms.
analysis.methods: The patient was treated with oral Valacyclovir, topical Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol, with close follow-up. The clinical course was monitored through subsequent visits to assess improvement and stabilization.
analysis.main_results: The patient had severe sub-acute ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. His VA was CF2ft, and IOP was 28. The SLE showed moderate conjunctival injection, corneal haze, inferior crescent shaped stromal infiltrate with CED of 2* 4 mm, and +2 mixed cells with flare. B-scan revealed a flat retina, no choroidal thickening, and quiet posterior segment. The patient reported improvement, but the clinical picture remained the same initially. One month later, CED was healed, and vision improved to 20\400 and 20\200. Cyclopentolate was switched to Cyclosporine, and the patient was stabilized by the 3-month mark.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as emphasizing the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings for early recognition and management of Monkeypox-related keratouveitis. They also highlighted the multimodal treatment methods of combining systemic and topical medications.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the need for vigilance in ocular settings when assessing patients with a history of Monkeypox, as well as the potential for multimodal treatment approaches in managing such cases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its case report design, which provides limited generalizability. However, the evidence is strong as it is based on direct clinical observations and follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis who presented with severe ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. The patient had a prior diagnosis of Monkeypox with skin manifestations. Clinical findings included corneal haze, stromal infiltrate, and mixed cells in the anterior chamber. The patient was treated with a combination of systemic and topical medications, including Valacyclovir, Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol. His vision improved over time, and he was stabilized by the 3-month mark. The authors emphasize the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings for early recognition and management of Monkeypox-related keratouveitis, as well as the value of multimodal treatment approaches. The study highlights the need for close follow-up and the potential for surgical intervention to improve visual outcomes. The evidence is strong due to direct clinical observations, but the case report design limits generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在突出猴痘相关角膜内炎患者的治疗干预和初步结果。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为一个病例报告,描述一名34岁男性患者因右眼猴痘相关角膜炎就诊并接受管理的情况。该患者在出现眼部症状前2个月曾因猴痘伴有皮肤表现而就诊。
elements_zh.methods: 患者接受了口服伐昔洛韦、局部环戊醇、莫西沙星和多佐胺/噻吗洛尔治疗,并进行了密切随访。通过后续就诊监测临床过程,以评估病情改善和稳定情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 患者出现了严重的亚急性眼部症状,包括肿胀、疼痛、畏光和视力下降。其视力为CF2ft,眼内压为28 mmHg。前房角膜后弹力层(SLE)显示中度结膜充血、角膜雾状混浊、下部新月形基质浸润,浸润范围为2*4 mm,前房中有+2级混合细胞伴房水闪辉。B超显示视网膜平坦,无脉络膜增厚,后段安静。患者报告症状有所改善,但初始临床表现未发生变化。一个月后,浸润范围已愈合,视力改善至20/400和20/200。环戊醇被更换为环孢素,患者在3个月时病情稳定。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调在眼科环境中详细询问病史对于早期识别和管理猴痘相关角膜内炎的重要性。他们还突出了多模式治疗方法,即结合全身和局部药物治疗。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为在评估有猴痘病史的患者时,在眼科环境中保持警惕提供依据,同时也可以为管理此类病例的多模式治疗方法提供参考。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受限于其病例报告设计,因此其推广性有限。然而,证据是强有力的,因为它基于直接的临床观察和随访。

papers.title: Pattern recognition receptors and divergent disease severity in zoonotic viral infections.
papers.abstract: Zoonotic viruses continue to emerge unpredictably, cross species barriers, and inflict major health, economic, and ecological burdens. Recent outbreaks of SARS-CoV-2, H5N1 avian influenza virus (AIV), monkeypox, and Zika virus underscore the unpredictability of viral emergence and the urgent need to understand host/pathogen interactions. This review focuses on how innate immune sensing via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) shapes disease severity across different species. While PRRs initiate antiviral defenses (interferons, ISGs), inflammatory cytokines, and programmed cell death, host outcomes diverge widely, shaped by genetic variation in PRR pathways and their regulators. Dysregulated inflammatory responses and inflammatory cell death can contribute substantially to severe disease independently of viral load, as demonstrated in influenza and coronavirus infections. Viral effectors that suppress or alter PRR signaling can show species-specific efficacy, and these mismatches can be critical determinants of disease when viruses jump hosts. Using avian influenza as an example, we highlight how disease outcomes vary with viral strain, host species, response timing, and tissue context. Overall, we propose that differential disease severity across host species reflects the balance among PRR-mediated resistance, the efficiency of viral immune evasion in the relevant host, and innate disease-tolerance mechanisms that limit tissue damage. Understanding these dynamics could enhance our ability to predict zoonotic emergence and mitigate the impact of viral pandemics.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on how innate immune sensing via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) shapes disease severity across different species. The central question is to understand the mechanisms underlying divergent disease outcomes in zoonotic viral infections, with a specific emphasis on the monkeypox virus.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It discusses the role of PRRs in antiviral defenses and highlights examples such as avian influenza and coronavirus infections to illustrate the concept.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that differential disease severity across host species reflects the balance among PRR-mediated resistance, the efficiency of viral immune evasion in the relevant host, and innate disease-tolerance mechanisms that limit tissue damage. It emphasizes that dysregulated inflammatory responses and inflammatory cell death can contribute substantially to severe disease, independent of viral load.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that host outcomes diverge widely, shaped by genetic variation in PRR pathways and their regulators. However, it does not provide specific evidence on the mechanisms of these variations or their impact on disease severity. The role of specific viral effectors in altering PRR signaling is also not clearly detailed.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Understanding these dynamics could enhance our ability to predict zoonotic emergence and mitigate the impact of viral pandemics. The review suggests that further research is needed to explore the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying PRR-mediated resistance and viral immune evasion in different host species.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores how pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) influence disease severity in zoonotic viral infections, with a focus on the monkeypox virus. It highlights the role of PRRs in initiating antiviral defenses, including interferons and inflammatory cytokines, and discusses how genetic variation in these pathways can lead to divergent host outcomes. The review emphasizes that dysregulated inflammatory responses and cell death can significantly contribute to severe disease, independent of viral load. It also notes that viral effectors altering PRR signaling can have species-specific impacts, which are critical in determining disease outcomes during host jumps. The findings suggest that understanding these mechanisms could improve our ability to predict zoonotic emergence and manage viral pandemics. However, the review identifies gaps in knowledge regarding the precise molecular and genetic factors that modulate PRR function and disease severity across species.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点探讨了模式识别受体(PRRs)介导的先天免疫感应如何在不同物种中影响疾病严重程度。核心问题是理解人兽共患病病毒感染中不同疾病结果的机制,特别强调猴痘病毒。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本综述是对现有文献的叙述性综合,没有明确提到系统性搜索方法、数据库或元分析。它讨论了PRRs在抗病毒药物抗病毒防御中的作用,并以禽流感和冠状病毒感染为例来说明这一概念。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 综述得出结论,不同宿主物种中不同的疾病严重程度反映了模式识别受体介导的抗性、病毒在相关宿主中免疫逃逸的效率以及限制组织损伤的先天疾病耐受机制之间的平衡。它强调失调的炎症反应和炎症性细胞死亡可以独立于病毒载量显著导致严重疾病。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 综述指出,宿主结果差异显著,这取决于PRRs通路及其调控因子的遗传变异。然而,它并未提供这些变异机制及其对疾病严重程度影响的具体证据。此外,特定病毒效应因子如何改变PRRs信号传导的作用也未明确阐述。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 理解这些动态变化可能有助于我们预测人兽共患病的出现并减轻病毒大流行的冲击。综述建议需要进一步研究以探索不同宿主物种中PRRs介导的抗性及病毒免疫逃逸的遗传和分子机制。

While PRRs initiate antiviral defenses (interferons, ISGs), inflammatory cytokines, and programmed cell death, host outcomes diverge widely, shaped by genetic variation in PRR pathways and their regulators. Dysregulated inflammatory responses and inflammatory cell death can contribute substantially to severe disease independently of viral load, as demonstrated in influenza and coronavirus infections. Viral effectors that suppress or alter PRR signaling can show species-specific efficacy, and these mismatches can be critical determinants of disease when viruses jump hosts. Using avian influenza as an example, we highlight how disease outcomes vary with viral strain, host species, response timing, and tissue context. Overall, we propose that differential disease severity across host species reflects the balance among PRR-mediated resistance, the efficiency of viral immune evasion in the relevant host, and innate disease-tolerance mechanisms that limit tissue damage. Understanding these dynamics could enhance our ability to predict zoonotic emergence and mitigate the impact of viral pandemics.
papers.abstract_zh: 人兽共患病病毒持续以不可预测的方式出现,跨越物种屏障,并造成重大的健康、经济和生态负担。最近对SARS-CoV-2、H5N1禽流感病毒(AIV)、猴痘和寨卡病毒的暴发突显了病毒出现的不可预测性以及迫切需要理解宿主/病原体相互作用的重要性。本综述重点探讨了模式识别受体(PRRs)介导的先天免疫感应如何在不同物种中影响疾病严重程度。尽管PRRs启动了抗病毒药物抗病毒防御(干扰素、ISGs)、炎症细胞因子和程序性细胞死亡,但宿主结果差异显著,这取决于PRRs通路及其调控因子的遗传变异。失调的炎症反应和炎症性细胞死亡可以独立于病毒载量显著导致严重疾病,如流感和冠状病毒感染所展示的。能够抑制或改变PRRs信号传导的病毒效应因子可能在不同物种中表现出特定的效果,这些不匹配可能是病毒跨物种溢出时疾病发生的关键决定因素。以禽流感为例,我们强调了疾病结果如何因病毒株、宿主物种、反应时机和组织背景而有所不同。总体而言,我们认为不同宿主物种中不同的疾病严重程度反映了模式识别受体介导的抗性、病毒在相关宿主中免疫逃逸的效率以及限制组织损伤的先天疾病耐受机制之间的平衡。理解这些动态变化可能有助于我们预测人兽共患病的出现并减轻病毒大流行的冲击。

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点探讨了模式识别受体(PRRs)介导的先天免疫感应如何在不同物种中影响疾病严重程度。核心问题是理解人兽共患病病毒感染中不同疾病结果的机制,特别强调猴痘病毒。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本综述是对现有文献的叙述性综合,没有明确提到系统性搜索方法、数据库或元分析。它讨论了PRRs在抗病毒药物抗病毒防御中的作用,并以禽流感和冠状病毒感染为例来说明这一概念。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 综述得出结论,不同宿主物种中不同的疾病严重程度反映了模式识别受体介导的抗性、病毒在相关宿主中免疫逃逸的效率以及限制组织损伤的先天疾病耐受机制之间的平衡。它强调失调的炎症反应和炎症性细胞死亡可以独立于病毒载量显著导致严重疾病。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 综述指出,宿主结果差异显著,这取决于PRRs通路及其调控因子的遗传变异。然而,它并未提供这些变异机制及其对疾病严重程度影响的具体证据。此外,特定病毒效应因子如何改变PRRs信号传导的作用也未明确阐述。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 理解这些动态变化可能有助于我们预测人兽共患病的出现并减轻病毒大流行的冲击。综述建议需要进一步研究以探索不同宿主物种中PRRs介导的抗性及病毒免疫逃逸的遗传和分子机制。

papers.full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. full_text_sections.full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). papers.title_original: Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a particular emphasis on the monkeypox virus (MPXV) and its clades. The central question is how to create antivirals that can target multiple RNA viruses, including MPXV, across different viral families and genera.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of antiviral drug development, drawing on advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing to understand viral diversity. It discusses the rationale for developing BSAs, provides an overview of approved and experimental antiviral agents, and outlines clinical development frameworks for evaluating such drugs, particularly in outbreak scenarios.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the development of BSAs is essential to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. It highlights the importance of broad-spectrum antivirals in the context of emerging viral threats, such as SARS-CoV-2, and emphasizes the need for a diversified portfolio of antivirals against RNA viruses.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the term 'broad-spectrum' antiviral lacks a clear definition and proposes the use of 'broader-spectrum' instead. It also highlights the limitations of some antiviral drugs, such as azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine, which were used in clinical trials with limited preclinical evidence. Additionally, it points out that the development of BSAs is still in its early stages and requires further research.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that fixed-dose combinations of antivirals, similar to those used in HIV treatment, could be ideal for combating multiple RNA viruses. It also emphasizes the importance of investing in antiviral drug discovery for both known and emerging viral threats, including MPXV, to improve preparedness and response capabilities.

analysis.summary_en: This review discusses the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, including the monkeypox virus (MPXV). It highlights the need for such drugs to address current unmet medical needs and enhance pandemic preparedness. The review outlines the rationale for BSAs, their potential applications in treating and preventing viral infections, and the challenges in defining and developing these agents. It also emphasizes the importance of fixed-dose combinations and sustained investment in antiviral research. The review notes that while some antivirals have shown promise, their efficacy and safety remain uncertain, underscoring the need for further studies and improved clinical frameworks.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本评论文章聚焦于针对RNA病毒的广谱直接作用抗病毒药物药物(BSAs)的开发,特别强调猴痘病毒(MPXV)及其亚型。核心问题是:如何开发能够针对不同病毒科和属的多种RNA病毒,包括MPXV的抗病毒药物药物?

elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论文章得出结论,开发BSAs对于应对当前未满足的医疗需求和加强流行病和大流行病的应对能力至关重要。它强调了在面对如SARS-CoV-2等新兴病毒威胁时,广谱抗病毒药物药物的重要性,并强调了针对RNA病毒开发多样化抗病毒药物药物的必要性。

analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论文章得出结论,开发BSAs对于应对当前未满足的医疗需求和加强流行病和大流行病的应对能力至关重要。它强调了在面对如SARS-CoV-2等新兴病毒威胁时,广谱抗病毒药物药物的重要性,并强调了针对RNA病毒开发多样化抗病毒药物药物的必要性。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本评论文章指出,'广谱' 抗病毒药物这一术语缺乏明确的定义,并建议使用'更广谱'一词。它还强调了一些抗病毒药物药物的局限性,例如阿奇霉素和羟氯喹,这些药物在临床试验中使用时缺乏充分的临床前证据。此外,它指出BSAs的开发仍处于早期阶段,需要进一步研究。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本评论文章建议,类似于HIV 治疗中使用的固定剂量组合,针对多种RNA病毒的抗病毒药物固定剂量组合可能是理想的解决方案。它还强调了对已知和新兴病毒威胁(包括MPXV)进行抗病毒药物药物发现投资的重要性,以提高应对和响应能力。

papers.title: Systematic Personnel Training as the Foundation for Biological Sovereignty in African Countries: Experience in Implementing Rospotrebnadzor Educational Programs for Specialists from the Republic of Burundi (2023–2025)
papers.abstract: The aim of the study was to describe the experience in introduction, systematization and thematic analysis of the implemented programs of the Rospotrebnadzor for specialists of the Republic of Burundi (2023–2025) in the field of laboratory diagnostics, epidemiological monitoring and biosafety as part of the strategy to strengthen the biological sovereignty of African states. Materials and methods. The study is based on the analysis of reporting documents and educational materials from 15 advanced training courses and field exercises conducted for the staff of the National Institute of Public Health of Burundi (INSP) in 2023–2025. The training was delivered in English using adapted educational programs. Descriptive statistics and content analysis of course topics were employed. Results and discussion. During the reporting period, 16 educational events were conducted, over 130 specialists were trained. The programs covered such key areas as: general laboratory practice and biosafety (PBA of II–IV pathogenicity groups), molecular diagnostics (including third-generation sequencing on the MinION platform and LAMP), serological screening (ELISA diagnostics of natural-focal and hepatotropic infections), bacteriology of food-borne infections, zoological and entomological surveillance, as well as specific pathology (HIV infection, mpox). In October 2024, field exercises using a mobile laboratory for indication and monitoring of particularly dangerous infections (MLIM) were carried out. It is shown that systemic transfer of competencies, rather than one-time equipment supplies, forms the basis for autonomous response to biological threats. The implemented programs have confirmed the effectiveness of systematic approach to personnel training as a tool for strengthening the national laboratory network. The coverage of modern diagnostic methods meets the current needs of the republic. The developed educational modules have potential for duplication in other developing African countries.

papers.title_zh: 系统性人员培训作为非洲国家生物主权的基础:布隆迪共和国专业人员实施俄罗斯联邦国家消费者权益保护和公共健康监督局(Rospotrebnadzor)教育项目的经验(2023–2025)
papers.source_body_en: The aim of the study was to describe the experience in introduction, systematization and thematic analysis of the implemented programs of the Rospotrebnadzor for specialists of the Republic of Burundi (2023–2025) in the field of laboratory diagnostics, epidemiological monitoring and biosafety as part of the strategy to strengthen the biological sovereignty of African states. Materials and methods. The study is based on the analysis of reporting documents and educational materials from 15 advanced training courses and field exercises conducted for the staff of the National Institute of Public Health of Burundi (INSP) in 2023–2025. The training was delivered in English using adapted educational programs. Descriptive statistics and content analysis of course topics were employed. Results and discussion. During the reporting period, 16 educational events were conducted, over 130 specialists were trained. The programs covered such key areas as: general laboratory practice and biosafety (PBA of II–IV pathogenicity groups), molecular diagnostics (including third-generation sequencing on the MinION platform and LAMP), serological screening (ELISA diagnostics of natural-focal and hepatotropic infections), bacteriology of food-borne infections, zoological and entomological surveillance, as well as specific pathology (HIV infection, mpox). In October 2024, field exercises using a mobile laboratory for indication and monitoring of particularly dangerous infections (MLIM) were carried out. It is shown that systemic transfer of competencies, rather than one-time equipment supplies, forms the basis for autonomous response to biological threats. The implemented programs have confirmed the effectiveness of systematic approach to personnel training as a tool for strengthening the national laboratory network. The coverage of modern diagnostic methods meets the current needs of the republic. The developed educational modules have potential for duplication in other developing African countries.

papers.title: Analysis of immediate upstream gene regions in orthopoxvirus genomes through the use of DNA Duplex Stability and explainable machine learning
papers.abstract: Orthopoxviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses with a temporally regulated gene expression program divided into early, intermediate, and late stages. Although many temporal gene functions are known, the promoter features that distinguish expression program require more precise characterization. Here, we employed an explainable machine learning approach to classify upstream gene regions as either early or non-early using the DNA Duplex Stability (DDS) as a numerical representation. We trained a Random Forest model on NCBI orthopoxvirus genomes and evaluated it using a public transcriptomic dataset of the agent Orthopoxvirus monkeypox virus (MPXV). To determine how individual features contributed to model predictions, we employed SHAP explainable Artificial Intelligence tool. Our results show that the region from -10 to -1 relative to the start codon is highly informative for class distinction. We found that the TAAAT-like motif at position -3 is a strong predictor of the non-early class, even in sequences originally labeled as early, providing insights into its multi-stage functionality. These findings provide an interpretable framework for identifying CDS proximal regions features linked to the temporal regulation of orthopoxvirus genes. This approach may support regulatory region annotation in newly sequenced genomes and help prioritize promoter variants affecting viral gene expression.

elements_zh.main_results: 结果显示,相对于起始密码子,从-10到-1的区域对于区分早期和非早期类别具有高度信息性。在位置-3处的TAAAT样基序被鉴定为预测非早期类别的强指标,即使在最初标记为早期的序列中也是如此。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现为识别与正痘病毒基因时间调控相关的编码序列(CDS)邻近区域特征提供了一个可解释的框架,为理解其多阶段功能提供了新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可能支持对新测序的基因组的调控区域注释,并有助于优先考虑影响病毒基因表达的启动子变体,这可能对理解与管理猴痘疾病具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于分析公共转录组数据集,未包括对模型预测的实验验证。由于依赖计算方法而没有直接的生物学测试,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Quarantine-associated viral pathogens in non-human primates: pathobiology, diagnostic surveillance, control strategies, and one health implications

papers.full_text: Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. This review compares national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examines pathogen-specific features, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. We emphasize the need for an integrated, risk-based approach incorporating longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, facility-level response procedures, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards. 4DiscussionRecent WHO pathogen prioritization efforts have emphasized family-level preparedness and response strategies (197). This concept is also relevant to NHP quarantine because many viruses of concern in primate colonies, particularly members of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, are capable of establishing persistent or latent infections (Table 2). In addition, other important pathogens, such as polyomaviruses and mycobacteria, may persist chronically after introduction. These biological features make complete elimination difficult. Moreover, NHP breeding and research facilities often rely on long-term group-housing systems, which may facilitate pathogen maintenance and transmission within colonies. Given that major NHP-associated viruses can be transmitted through horizontal and, in some cases, vertical routes, the introduction of infected animals may increase the likelihood of transmission to other animals within the colony (Table 3). Therefore, family-level diagnostic preparedness, continuous surveillance, and internationally coordinated quarantine practices are important for NHP facilities.Table 2Quarantine-associated viruses in microbiological monitoring because many NHP-associated viruses generally cause asymptomatic or only mild infections, although various clinical manifestations may occasionally occur (Figure 2). Nevertheless, microbiological surveillance standards differ among countries, and enforceable requirements remain limited. Given that NHPs are commonly distributed from a limited number of breeding facilities to research institutions worldwide, effective quarantine should be addressed not only at the level of individual facilities but also harmonized international standards and coordinated surveillance (18). From a One Health perspective, there is a need to define a minimum set of diseases for quarantine screening, particularly latent or persistent viral infections and tuberculosis, to reduce the risks associated with the international movement of NHPs. Their potential for subclinical infection and zoonotic transmission further highlights the importance of integrated surveillance for NHP colony health, occupational safety, research reliability, and public health (Figure 3). However, important knowledge gaps remain regarding transmission dynamics in NHP research and facility settings and the associated risks to humans. The current evidence base is also limited by uneven species coverage, heterogeneity among institutions and surveillance practices, and insufficient data for certain viral pathogens. Given these uncertainties, a precautionary approach based on a minimum level of routine surveillance is warranted to reduce the risk of undetected infection and transmission. Considering the variability in screening practices among institutions and the limitations of direct antigen or pathogen detection for many retroviruses and herpesviruses, we propose that this minimum surveillance framework should include at least annual antibody testing for major persistent or latent viruses, including SIV, SRV, STLV, B virus, SCMV, and SVV.Figure 2Differential diagnostic overview of quarantine-associated major viral diseases in non-human primates by clinical presentation and host group. Comparison of major viruses infecting African NHPs and macaques according to human infectivity, subclinical and persistent infection in NHPs, and fatality in humans. SIV, simian immunodeficiency virus; STLV, simian T-cell lymphotropic virus; SVV, simian varicella virus; SCMV, simian cytomegalovirus; SV40, simian virus 40.Diagram comparing viruses infecting African nonhuman primates and macaques according to their potential for human infection, persistence in nonhuman primates, and fatal outcomes in humans. Among viruses infecting African nonhuman primates, SIV and STLV can infect humans but are not shown as directly fatal. Among macaque viruses, B virus, SIV, STLV, and SV40 can infect humans; B virus, STLV, and SV40 are associated with subclinical or persistent infection in nonhuman primates, while B virus is highlighted as potentially fatal in humans.In addition to determining seropositivity using established diagnostic cut-off values, longitudinal evaluation of antibody titers, rather than reliance on a single time-point measurement, may be important for assessing infection status and identifying changes associated with exposure, viral reactivation, or potential transmission within a colony. Antibody results should also be evaluated beyond the individual animal level, with comparisons among groups, housing rooms, and facilities to identify temporal changes in exposure and transmission patterns. Nevertheless, antibody testing should not be used in isolation. Serological findings should be interpreted together with clinical observation, necropsy findings, antigen or molecular assays, hematological and serum biochemical data, and expert interpretation. Because infected animals may exhibit only mild or no apparent clinical signs and viral shedding may be intermittent, repeated antigen or molecular testing of animals with suspected infection or positive serological findings may be necessary to confirm active viral shedding.Furthermore, facility-level standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be established in advance for each pathogen to define appropriate response measures according to different combinations of diagnostic results, such as seropositivity alone or concurrent positive serological and antigen or molecular findings. The detection of these pathogens should prompt the implementation of appropriate SOPs to prevent further transmission within the colony, restrict the transfer of infected or exposed animals, and protect personnel from zoonotic exposure. For high-risk zoonotic agents such as B virus, rapid post-exposure evaluation and appropriate antiviral prophylaxis or treatment are particularly important to reduce the risk of severe human disease. Thus, SOPs, routine training, exposure-response plans, and access to appropriate medical countermeasures should be established before incidents occur.In addition to viruses of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, four viral diseases of particular concern were also included because of their high pathogenicity in humans and recent public health importance. Although NHPs are not generally considered natural reservoirs for these viruses, they may become infected as susceptible or incidental hosts and therefore warrant consideration during quarantine. Because these infections can cause recognizable clinical signs in macaques, as in humans, careful clinical surveillance is important during the quarantine period. Unlike persistent or latent viral infections, quarantine surveillance for Marburg virus, Ebola virus, MPXV, and rabies virus should focus on the early recognition of suggestive clinical signs, followed by the implementation of appropriate precautionary biosafety measures before prompt diagnostic testing using antigen or molecular assays and, when necessary, postmortem examination. Rapid identification of suspected or confirmed cases should then trigger appropriate public health and facility-level response measures, including assessment and management of potentially exposed personnel, isolation of affected animals, and measures to prevent further transmission. 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. Geographical locations of documented NHP viral infections and outbreaks reported in the literature; circles, documented natural or captive infections; triangles, reported outbreaks; different colors, individual viruses; locations based on published reports, not necessarily representing the complete geographical distribution or prevalence of each virus. Detailed information on documented infections and outbreaks, including corresponding references, Supplementary Table S1 (127, 162, 179, 182, 198–210).World map showing the geographic distribution of documented cases and endemic or natural infections of twelve viruses affecting nonhuman primates, using color-coded circles for outbreaks and triangles for endemic regions, with a legend identifying each virus.Experimental NHPs are typically outbred and exhibit greater genetic diversity than many inbred preclinical animal models (16). This heterogeneity may lead to individual variation in susceptibility to infectious agents. Outdoor housing and husbandry practices can further hinder the establishment and maintenance of SPF colonies (17). Therefore, appropriate quarantine procedures are essential for NHPs. This review provides an overview of national quarantine protocols and major viral pathogens relevant to NHPs. We focus on pathogen biology and epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, and interventions, and consider their implications for risk-based quarantine, surveillance, and infection-control strategies. full_text_sections.abstract: Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. This review compares national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examines pathogen-specific features, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. We emphasize the need for an integrated, risk-based approach incorporating longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, facility-level response procedures, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards.
full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionRecent WHO pathogen prioritization efforts have emphasized family-level preparedness and response strategies (197). This concept is also relevant to NHP quarantine because many viruses of concern in primate colonies, particularly members of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, are capable of establishing persistent or latent infections (Table 2). In addition, other important pathogens, such as polyomaviruses and mycobacteria, may persist chronically after introduction. These biological features make complete elimination difficult. Moreover, NHP breeding and research facilities often rely on long-term group-housing systems, which may facilitate pathogen maintenance and transmission within colonies. Given that major NHP-associated viruses can be transmitted through horizontal and, in some cases, vertical routes, the introduction of infected animals may increase the likelihood of transmission to other animals within the colony (Table 3). full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. Geographical locations of documented NHP viral infections and outbreaks reported in the literature; circles, documented natural or captive infections; triangles, reported outbreaks; different colors, individual viruses; locations based on published reports, not necessarily representing the complete geographical distribution or prevalence of each virus. Detailed information on documented infections and outbreaks, including corresponding references, Supplementary Table S1 (127, 162, 179, 182, 198–210).World map showing the geographic distribution of documented cases and endemic or natural infections of twelve viruses affecting nonhuman primates, using color-coded circles for outbreaks and triangles for endemic regions, with a legend identifying each virus.Experimental NHPs are typically outbred and exhibit greater genetic diversity than many inbred preclinical animal models (16). This heterogeneity may lead to individual variation in susceptibility to infectious agents. Outdoor housing and husbandry practices can further hinder the establishment and maintenance of SPF colonies (17). Therefore, appropriate quarantine procedures are essential for NHPs. This review provides an overview of national quarantine protocols and major viral pathogens relevant to NHPs. We focus on pathogen biology and epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, and interventions, and consider their implications for risk-based quarantine, surveillance, and infection-control strategies. We also highlight the need for coordinated facility-level responses, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards from a One Health perspective. 2International quarantine policies and virus surveillance in NHPs facilities2.1Republic of KoreaIn the Republic of Korea, the importation of NHPs is regulated under the Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases, and these species are classified as designated quarantine animals subject to mandatory veterinary inspection upon importation. Experimental macaques, primarily cynomolgus (Macaca fascicularis) and rhesus (Macaca mulatta) macaques, are predominantly imported from Asian countries, including China, Vietnam, and Cambodia (10, 18). Imported NHPs must undergo at least 30 days of pre-export quarantine under the supervision of a government-designated veterinarian in the exporting country, followed by an additional 30-day quarantine at a designated national animal quarantine facility in Korea prior to release for research use. Specific sanitary import requirements are defined in the national import health regulations for NHP species (19). These regulations require that the exporting country be free from Ebola virus and Marburg virus diseases. The breeding facility of origin must have no evidence of clinical, serological, or pathological occurrence of measles, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, monkeypox, or tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis and M. bovis) for at least 24 months prior to export. During the mandatory pre-export quarantine period, NHPs must be confirmed negative for tuberculosis, internal and external parasites, and enteric bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., and Yersinia spp. Tuberculosis screening must include at least one tuberculin skin test (TST) conducted within one week after the start of quarantine, while hepatitis B virus testing is additionally required for gibbons and great apes.Beyond these national regulatory mandates, research institutions often conduct additional microbiological screening. However, the pathogens targeted for screening vary according to facility policies, research objectives, and biosafety requirements. Additional screening may include testing for B virus, SIV, STLV, SRV, and other facility-specific pathogens.2.2United statesIn the United States, the importation of NHPs is regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under the Public Health Service Act (20). All imported NHPs must undergo quarantine for a minimum of 31 days in a CDC-registered facility prior to release. At the federal regulatory level, tuberculosis surveillance via serial TST is the only routine laboratory test universally required during quarantine. Each NHP must receive at least three TSTs administered on the eyelid using mammalian old tuberculin (MOT), at intervals of at least 2 weeks. Reactions must be evaluated at 24, 48, and 72 h after each test. Routine laboratory screening for other diseases is not uniformly required, although additional diagnostic testing may be required under specific clinical circumstances, including filovirus testing in Old World NHPs exhibiting clinical signs suggestive of filovirus disease.Beyond federal requirements, individual research institutions may implement additional quarantine measures based on their own policies. For example, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) requires documentation of a negative TST within 30 days prior to shipment (21).
