supplementary_news.content: Bulgaria World Opinions Business Properties Auto Tech Sport Culture Bulgaria World Opinions Business Properties Auto Tech Sport Culture Cars Properties Jobs Small ads Здраве » Медицина » Hong Kong monkeypox cases surge Link to main version Oct 11, 2026 07:14 120 Hong Kong monkeypox cases surge 21 new cases since August, accounting for 70% of all infections in 2026. Health authorities expand vaccination among at-risk groups Снимка: YouTube Maria Atanasova Author at Fakti.bg Hong Kong has seen a sharp rise in monkeypox cases. There have been 21 new infections since August, accounting for 70% of the city's 30 cases in 2026, the Centre for Health Protection said. Since the start of the year, 23 of the cases have been local and seven have been imported. The latest confirmed case is a 29-year-old man. He first developed a rash on his buttocks on September 28, followed by a rash on his limbs, fever and swollen lymph nodes. Medical staff identified his symptoms on October 8 during a visit to a mobile vaccination station. The man has been sent for isolation and treatment at Princess Margaret Hospital and is in stable condition. Multiple chains of transmission The epidemiological study shows that all 21 patients diagnosed since August reported high-risk sexual contacts during the incubation period. Among the circumstances mentioned are contacts with unknown men, more than one partner and sex without a condom. Most of those infected have not been vaccinated. Genetic analysis of the virus has identified identical genetic sequences in some of the cases. According to the Center for Health Protection, this may point to a common source of infection, while in the community of men who have sex with men, several separate chains of transmission are likely to be operating. More than half of the patients have used dating apps to find casual sexual partners in recent months. In some cases, new contacts cannot be traced after diagnosis, making it difficult to track and take action. Vaccination expanded “The center again urges people who have had high-risk sexual contacts, especially with strangers, to be vigilant, get vaccinated against monkeypox and avoid risky contacts,“ health authorities said. In the past two weeks, about 360 people from risk groups have received the vaccine. In early October, the number of doses administered was more than 70% higher than the same period the previous month. Health authorities are adding new vaccination sites and times and are running an information campaign through dating apps and organizations working with at-risk groups. Since 2022, 114 cases of monkeypox have been reported in Hong Kong, all of whom are male. The center emphasizes that the disease is not usually transmitted through the air or through respiratory droplets, and the main risk is through close physical contact. If a rash, fever, chills or enlarged lymph nodes appear, health authorities urge those affected to seek medical attention and avoid contact with other people. Sources: scmp.com, news.tvb.com China

Search Spanish News / Health / Hospital Mpox Death Puts San Sebastián Protocol Under Scrutiny 6 mins read Published October 9, 2026, 2:40 PM Hospital Mpox Death Puts San Sebastián Protocol Under Scrutiny Post by Richard Reid Hospital Mpox Death Puts San Sebastián Protocol Under Scrutiny © russpain.com Share Facebook X WhatsApp Copy link Reddit A 61-year-old cancer patient died after contracting Mpox at Hospital Donostia. More than 30 contacts are under medical surveillance as Osakidetza defends its response. The patient had spent weeks at Hospital Donostia in San Sebastián while being treated for cancer and was already immunosuppressed. He later died after contracting Mpox during his stay. This is the first death in Euskadi involving the infection. Doctors have not definitively established that Mpox directly caused it. Euskadi’s Department of Health considered it highly likely that the infection contributed to the death, while the official account has not identified Mpox as the sole or direct cause. The man shared a room for several days with another patient whose positive diagnosis was confirmed later. He had initially been admitted with a throat complication and did not show the characteristic skin lesions associated with Mpox. Early tests pointed to another infection, so he received antibiotics before further testing identified the virus. That atypical presentation matters in an immunocompromised hospital patient. Without visible lesions, recognition and isolation can be delayed. The San Sebastián death was reported as the third Mpox-related death in Spain in 2026; the two earlier patients were living with HIV. The hospital says it applied the protocol correctly. Reports from RTVE and other Spanish media say the available evidence does not establish a deliberate breach of hospital procedures. Osakidetza maintains that the two men were not together after the infection became known. Its guidance requires a patient with Mpox to remain in an individual room with a private bathroom until the lesions disappear or the patient is discharged. After discharge, physical contact and sexual relations should be avoided until the skin has completely healed. Miguel Ángel Goenaga, head of Infectious Diseases at Hospital Donostia, said home isolation is normally preferred. The patient believed to have transmitted the infection was discharged after his condition improved and is now being monitored at home. He is reported to be in good health. The family says the patient was recovering from planned surgery for a throat tumour and that Osakidetza told them Mpox had begun on 16 September, roughly four to five days before symptoms appeared. This account differs from the hospital’s formulation and has not resolved the chronology of the infection. The patient’s family The exact route of transmission inside the hospital remains unknown. Goenaga said such transmission is uncommon. He suggested that the men might have come into contact at night or shared an object. The victim’s relatives told the newspaper that he spent less than a week with the other patient and had been undergoing rehabilitation before contracting the virus. They also said staff began wearing masks in the room without initially explaining why. According to the family, they were informed two days later after repeatedly asking about the situation. The room was then disinfected. More than 30 people, including relatives and healthcare workers, have been identified as close contacts and vaccinated or placed under follow-up. Osakidetza said approximately 30 people who had close contact with the two infected patients were offered vaccination and medical monitoring. The monitoring will last 21 days. Contacts must check their temperature and watch for skin lesions. Those lesions can pass through several stages before forming and shedding a scab. The family’s account and the official explanation leave the central issue unresolved: how the virus crossed between patients despite the hospital’s stated procedures. The case was also covered in an earlier report by Russpain. Health officials say the man had very serious illnesses. They also say a bacterial infection present before Mpox probably played the main role in his final deterioration. Oskar Ortiz de Guinea said any infection can worsen the condition of an immunosuppressed patient. The death occurred on Tuesday evening. The Department of Health has confirmed it while maintaining that Mpox’s precise medical contribution has not been definitively established. Mpox spreads through close contact between people or between animals and people. Its incubation period ranges from five to 21 days. Common symptoms include fever and headache. Muscle pain, swollen lymph nodes, exhaustion and a rash can follow, with the rash spreading from the face to other parts of the body. Goenaga described transmission as limited and said mortality from the virus is below 5%. He also characterised transmission within a hospital as rare. Osakidetza considers new cases linked to the hospital incident highly unlikely after preventive measures were activated. Euskadi recorded 299 cases by the end of last September, while Spain recorded 10,535. In the Basque Country, six cases were identified in 2025. There were 35 during the first nine months of this year: eight in Gipuzkoa, 21 in Bizkaia and six in Álava. The authorities say every recorded case in Euskadi received vaccination and medical follow-up. Reports published by El Mundo and Sur in English put the cumulative number for the Basque Country at 245 since the beginning of the global outbreak in 2022. They also confirm the 35 cases recorded in 2026. The figures use different reporting cut-offs and should not be treated as interchangeable without clarification. Mpox emerged in human medicine in 1970 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spread globally during outbreaks in 2022. In San Sebastián, an immunosuppressed patient became infected in hospital, the transmission route remains unknown, and more than 30 contacts are being monitored. Osakidetza’s defence of the protocol fits the facts presented. The unexplained transmission between patients has focused attention on individual isolation and early recognition of atypical symptoms. Prompt communication is also part of the infection-control response. Available reports describe the case as a lesson for hospital screening, but do not report any formal revision of Osakidetza’s protocol. "I have decided that the global #monkeypox outbreak represents a public health emergency of international concern," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said at a press conference. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source He said a committee of experts who met yesterday was unable to reach a consensus, so it fell on him to decide whether to trigger the highest alert possible. Read more Anyone can drown; no one should "WHO's assessment is that the risk of monkeypox is moderate globally and in all regions, except in the European region where we assess the risk as high," he added. Monkeypox has affected over 15,800 people in 72 countries, according to a tally by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published on July 20. The first symptoms of monkeypox are fever, headaches, muscle pain and back pain during the course of five days. Rashes subsequently appear on the face, the palms of hands and soles of feet, followed by lesions, spots and finally scabs. Read more Four die of Covid, 446 new cases logged A surge in monkeypox infections has been reported since early May outside the West and Central African countries where the disease has long been endemic. On June 23, the WHO convened an emergency committee (EC) of experts to decide if monkeypox constitutes a so-called Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) -- the UN health agency's highest alert level. But a majority advised Tedros that the situation, at that point, had not met the threshold. The second meeting was called on Thursday with case numbers rising further, where Tedros said he was worried. "I need your advice in assessing the immediate and mid-term public health implications," Tedros told the meeting, which lasted more than six hours. A US health expert sounded a grim warning late on Friday. "Since the last #monkeypox EC just weeks ago, we've seen an exponential rise in cases. It's inevitable that cases will dramatically rise in the coming weeks & months. That's why @DrTedros must sound the global alarm," Lawrence Gostin, the director of the WHO Collaborating Center on National and Global Health Law, said on Twitter. "A failure to act will have grave consequences for global health." A viral infection resembling smallpox and first detected in humans in 1970, monkeypox is less dangerous and contagious than smallpox, which was eradicated in 1980. Ninety-five percent of cases have been transmitted through sexual activity, according to a study of 528 people in 16 countries published in the New England Journal of Medicine -- the largest research to date. Read more Might metformin protect against hepatocellular carcinoma? Overall, 98 percent of infected people were gay or bisexual men, and around a third were known to have visited sex-on-site venues such as sex parties or saunas within the previous month. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. The European Union's drug watchdog on Friday recommended for approval the use of Imvanex, a smallpox vaccine, to treat monkeypox. Imvanex, developed by Danish drugmaker Bavarian Nordic, has been approved in the EU since 2013 for the prevention of smallpox. It was also considered a potential vaccine for monkeypox because of the similarity between the monkeypox virus and the smallpox virus. supplementary_news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 12, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Editorial Mpox threat Isolation guidance also needs to reach households clearly Editorial October 08, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email Sindh's growing mpox caseload requires a more visible and organised public-health response before sporadic infections become harder to contain. The province has recorded 93 confirmed cases this year and 11 deaths, while the recent rise is particularly concerning. Twenty cases were reported in September and another six have already emerged in October. Karachi has recorded the highest number, followed by Khairpur and Sukkur. The numbers remain relatively small compared with those of some other infectious diseases, but that is precisely why containment must begin early. Sindh's immediate priority must be stronger case detection. Doctors at public and private hospitals and emergency departments should be able to recognise suspected cases quickly and report them through the provincial surveillance system without delay. Laboratories must have sufficient capacity to return results promptly. Every confirmed infection should trigger careful contact tracing so that exposed individuals can be monitored and advised before another chain of transmission develops. Isolation guidance also needs to reach households clearly. Pakistan's national guidelines call for infected people to remain separated from others until their rash has healed, the scabs have fallen off and a fresh layer of skin has formed. Vaccination should also form part of the preparedness strategy, but it must be targeted. WHO does not recommend indiscriminate mass vaccination. It advises prioritising people at greater risk of exposure, including close contacts of confirmed patients and healthcare personnel handling cases. Pakistan should assess available stocks and access to international supply mechanisms before a larger outbreak creates an urgent scramble for doses. Mpox is containable. What turns a manageable outbreak into a wider public-health problem is delayed diagnosis and weak surveillance coupled with complacency between individual cases. Sindh still has the opportunity to interrupt transmission while the numbers remain limited. supplementary_news.content: TODAY’S PAPER | October 12, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Sindh 11 deaths, 93 mpox cases reported in Sindh 70 men, 23 women as well as children up to the age of nine tested positive Faran Khan October 07, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email The image shows Mpox micrograph in the background. PHOTO: PIXABAY KARACHI: Sindh has reported 93 confirmed cases of mpox so far this year, with 11 deaths attributed to the viral disease, according to the latest report of the Provincial Disease Surveillance and Response Unit's (PDSRU) laboratory surveillance network. Of the 93 confirmed cases, 70 were men, accounting for 75.27 per cent, while 23 were women. People aged 30 to 39 were the most affected age group, with 26 confirmed cases, while 23 children up to the age of nine also tested positive for mpox. April recorded the highest number of cases at 31, followed by September with 20, August 17, July seven, October six so far, March five, June four and May two. Meanwhile, a 50-year-old man from Nawabshah was suspected of having mpox on Monday and was shifted in critical condition to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital in NIPA, Karachi, where he was admitted to the intensive care unit. Hospital officials said the patient had rashes on his hands and feet, raising suspicion of mpox. Samples were collected for further diagnostic and laboratory testing. Experts said mpox is a viral disease that can spread through close physical or skin-to-skin contact with an infected person, as well as contact with lesions, bodily fluids or contaminated objects. Common symptoms include fever, headache, body aches, weakness, swollen lymph nodes and skin rashes or blisters. (Iñigo Royo) Oskar Ortiz de Guinea 09/10/2026 a las 07:52h. The only thing clear to the family of the man who died on Tuesday after contracting mpox at Donostia Hospital is that their loved one is gone, that he died on Tuesday, and that he did not die from the throat tumour for which he was admitted on 1 September to undergo a scheduled laryngectomy. Furthermore, they maintain that his post-operative recovery, despite bleeding that required two further operations, was progressing well. 'He had started rehabilitation in the hospital gymnasium, and the speech therapist had told him that speech therapy would begin in October,' his closest relatives explained, passing the telephone between them. One recalled: 'Two days before his symptoms began, a doctor told me that whilst he had not been before, he was now out of danger.' Relatives of the first person to die after contracting mpox in the Basque Country were at the chapel of rest yesterday midday holding a vigil for the victim when they were shocked to see his case published on the website of this newspaper. They did not expect the news to reach the press so soon, nor to find themselves in this predicament prematurely. 'We have to think about what to do, what action to take,' they said, though they already have an appointment with a solicitor later this month. For them, 'what is clear' is that the victim—who was 61 years old and 'it is true that he had suffered an infection', as confirmed by Osakidetza (the Basque Health Service)—'was admitted for a scheduled laryngectomy, was recovering, and suddenly everything deteriorated because he contracted mpox after sharing a room with an infected patient without any preventive measures being taken.' The family spent Thursday at the wake and, understandably distressed, did not wish to dwell in detail on the chronology of events over the five weeks spent at Donostia Hospital. 'We have records with the dates,' they noted. In broad terms, they recalled that the victim was admitted on 1 September for surgery. On that day, he already shared a room with patient zero, who, according to them, was suffering from 'headaches, a sore throat...' Healthcare workers in masks In all, both patients shared a room for 'less than a week'. Following an initial few days of 'normal' coexistence between two patients sharing a room, healthcare staff suddenly began wearing face masks. 'First a nursing assistant put one on, and we thought she had a cold or Covid. But then we noticed the other nurses were wearing them too. We asked at the nursing station, and they told us not to worry. His family were wearing masks, but nobody told us anything.' They state that 'two days' later, and 'after much persistence', it was confirmed to them that the roommate had tested positive and 'he was discharged' to isolate at home. The room was subsequently disinfected. They maintain that the deceased shared the room with four other patients. In the days that followed, the man suffered complications involving bleeding and an infection, 'something we had already been told was to be expected. Mpox was not.' He underwent two further operations and began to recover. 'Two days after' things started looking up, he began experiencing such severe headaches that 'one night he required morphine', and 'two or three days later spots appeared on his forehead. He was assessed by an infectious disease specialist and an internist, who noticed lesions on his palms.' He was isolated in the infectious diseases unit, 'but they realised it was better to treat his throat and transferred him back to the other ward.' As his condition 'worsened', he was admitted 'to intensive care. And despite antibiotics, antivirals, morphine and other treatments, he did not recover.' Newsletter A call from Osakidetza pinpointed the onset of mpox 'on 16 September', which they were told was 'four or five days before the symptoms appeared'.
